processing: Same-day processing of one bud with one or two leaves: sorting, fixing, rolling, sieving, a first pan-grinding, cooling, a second pan-grinding, then removing dust and grading. The two rounds of drying in the pan give the tea its name.
harvest_season: One bud with one or two leaves, picked and processed the same day. The season is not spelled out; spring is the prized picking for green teas of this kind.
appearance_dry: Plump, tight strips with sharp tips, glossy blue-green with visible white down and a few tender stems.
appearance_wet: Plump, tender, even leaves of a bright green.
taste_profile: A rich young-leaf aroma with a fresh, brisk and full-bodied cup, weightier than most eastern Chinese greens.

brewing.notes: Advice as for other Yunnan large-leaf greens: water a little off the boil and short steeps, since this leaf has plenty of strength.

vintage_note: Sold as a green tea of the current year, as is usual for its class, and best drunk within about a year. It has no ageing tradition. It is a local Tengchong tea, so expect to find it mainly in the region or from sellers who deal directly with it.
description:
This is a green tea from Qingliang Mountain in Puchuan township, Tengchong, in far-western Yunnan. The name means pan-ground tea, and that step is what sets it apart.

The mountain faces the Longchuan River and rises to around 2,000 metres, with frequent drizzle and cloud and loose, sandy yellow soil. Large-leaf shoots are picked and worked the same day. After fixing and rolling, the leaf is ground in the hot pan twice with a cooling rest between, which tightens it into firm, pointed strips.

In the cup it is bright yellow-green, with a rich young-leaf aroma and a fresh, full taste. It carries more body than a Zhejiang green, so treat it gently: water a little off the boil, short steeps, and no leaving the leaf to stew.

Good leaf should look tight, even and glossy with visible down. The Qingliangshan name is also a registered trademark, so read the producer on the packet and not just the words Moguo tea, which are used more loosely.
history:
Tea growing in Puchuan is old enough that a large tea tree said to be more than 300 years old still stands in the township. The modern industry owes much to Li Genyuan, a local figure who in the 1930s brought in tea specialists from Jiangsu and opened a tea school to train technicians.

The tea itself has been recognised at provincial level, with Yunnan gold and silver tea awards and a provincial science and technology prize mentioned in local accounts, though without dates.
